section.title: Crossing the Red Sea
section.sectionRationale: This is the decisive act of deliverance that gives Israel its identity as a redeemed people: trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, they watch the LORD fight for them and walk through the waters on dry ground. The New Testament treats this event as the paradigm for understanding salvation itself.
section.thesis: Cornered between the sea and Pharaoh's army, Israel is told to stand still and watch the LORD fight for them; He divides the sea, brings them through on dry ground, and destroys the pursuing army, so that Israel finally fears the LORD and believes in Him and in Moses His servant.
section.frameNote: Five movements: God's guidance by the longer road and the pillar of cloud and fire; Pharaoh's pursuit; Israel's terror and Moses' word of faith; the sea divided and crossed; and the sea returning to destroy the Egyptians while Israel believes.

units.label: God leads by the longer road
units.note: the pillar of cloud and fire

media.alt: A pillar of cloud by day and fire by night leading the people
media.caption: The LORD Himself goes before them, by day and by night.

verses.text: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.”
So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle.

Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.”
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness.
And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night.
Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites to turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. You are to encamp by the sea, directly opposite Baal-zephon.
For Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.’

And I will harden Pharaoh's heart so that he will pursue them. But I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” 
So this is what the Israelites did.
When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them and said, “What have we done? We have released Israel from serving us.”
So Pharaoh prepared his chariot and took his army with him.
He took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them.
And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt so that he pursued the Israelites, who were marching out defiantly.
The Egyptians, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots, horsemen and troops, pursued the Israelites and overtook them as they camped by the sea near Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon.

units.label: Israel's fear, Moses' word of faith
units.note: stand still and see the salvation of the LORD

verses.text: As Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them, and they were terrified and cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us into the wilderness to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt?
Did we not say to you in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone so that we may serve the Egyptians’? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.”

But Moses told the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD's {{salvation|salvation}}, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.
The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.”
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.
And as for you, lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground.
And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them. Then I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army and chariots and horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I am honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.”
And the angel of God, who had gone before the camp of Israel, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from before them and stood behind them,
so that it came between the camps of Egypt and Israel. The cloud was there in the darkness, but it lit up the night. So all night long neither camp went near the other.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided,
and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left.
And the Egyptians chased after them, all Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen, and followed them into the sea.
At morning watch, however, the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion.
He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving. “Let us flee from the Israelites,” said the Egyptians, “for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!”
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.”
So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. As the Egyptians were retreating, the LORD swept them into the sea.
The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen, the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived.
But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left.
That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore.
When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people {{feared|feared}} the LORD and {{believed|believed}} in Him and in His servant Moses.

salvation.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. The word shares its root with the name Joshua and, in Greek translation, lies behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves. Moses tells the terrified people to stand and watch this yeshuah unfold, a salvation they cannot achieve, only receive.

feared.gloss: To fear, to stand in reverent awe. After watching the LORD destroy Pharaoh's army, Israel's fear moves from terror of Egypt to reverence for God, the beginning of true worship.

believed.gloss: To believe, to trust, to be firm or faithful, root of the word amen. Israel's fear and faith are named together as the fruit of watching God act; belief here is not blind but grounded in what they had just seen Him do.

basic.context: Israel is trapped, the sea ahead, Pharaoh's army closing in behind. They panic and blame Moses, but Moses tells them to stand still and watch God save them. The LORD splits the sea, Israel walks through on dry ground, and the returning waters destroy the pursuing army completely.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historical deliverance of a real, historical people at a real body of water. The New Testament treats it as the Old Testament's clearest picture of salvation: helpless people, an impossible barrier, and a God who fights and delivers when His people can do nothing but trust and obey.
basic.originalLanguages: Moses promises Israel they will see the LORD's yeshuah, salvation, using the very word later behind the names Joshua and Jesus. Watching God's power destroy Egypt, Israel finally yare, fears, the LORD rightly, and they aman, believe, trust Him, the same root behind the word amen.
basic.typology: Paul later calls this crossing a baptism into Moses, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, an image the New Testament reapplies to baptism into Christ: passing through death-dealing waters into new life on the other side, while judgment falls on those left behind.
basic.christ: Just as Israel could only stand still and watch the LORD fight for them, salvation in Christ comes not by human effort but by trusting a Mediator who fights the real battle and wins it alone. The New Testament reads this whole episode as inviting a Christ-centered lens: get out of bondage, cross over by grace, all through a mediator's action, not your own.
basic.god: God is a warrior who fights for His helpless people, and He is also a God whose glory is displayed precisely in defeating those who oppose Him. His patience with Israel's fear and grumbling is matched by His relentless commitment to bring them all the way through.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 10:1-2 calls this a baptism into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Isaiah 51:9-11 recalls this crossing as the pattern for future redemption. Psalm 106:7-12 retells the story to teach later generations to trust God's saving power.
basic.oneStory: Cornered with no way out, Israel does nothing but stand still while God alone fights and saves. This becomes the Bible's template for salvation itself: helpless sinners, an impossible barrier, and a God who acts decisively through a mediator, ultimately fulfilled when Christ alone secures the deliverance His people could never achieve themselves.

context.literary:
The account runs from Exodus 13:17 to 14:31 and is followed at once by the Song of the Sea in chapter 15, so that the event is told twice, first in prose and then in poetry. The prose is built in panels, each opened by a word from the LORD: 'Then the LORD said to Moses,' Exodus 14:1, 14:15 and 14:26. Each speech is followed by its fulfilment. God says Pharaoh will pursue, and he does, verses 4 to 9. God says Moses is to stretch out his hand and divide the sea, and he does, verses 16 and 21. God says the waters will return, and they do, verses 26 to 28. The narrative is showing that every stage is directed by the LORD's word.

Two phrases act as bookends. 'The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' verses 4 and 18, states the purpose at the start and middle. 'Israel saw' closes the account, verses 30 and 31: they saw the Egyptians dead on the shore, and they saw the great power of the LORD. The Israelites who at the start 'looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them,' verse 10, end by seeing the same Egyptians dead. Moses' promise in verse 13, 'you will see the LORD's salvation... the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again,' is exactly fulfilled.

The description of the crossing is deliberately repetitive. 'On dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left' appears in verse 22 and again in verse 29, framing the destruction of the army between them. The effect is to hold two pictures side by side: the same waters that stood as walls for Israel returned as a flood for Egypt.

The passage also turns on reversals of fear. In verse 10 Israel is 'terrified' of the Egyptians. In verse 25 the Egyptians say 'Let us flee from the Israelites.' In verse 31 Israel 'feared the LORD.' Fear of Pharaoh gives way to the fear of God, which is the movement the whole book traces, from service to Pharaoh to the service of the LORD.
context.historical:
God did not take Israel by 'the road through the land of the Philistines,' Exodus 13:17, the main coastal route from Egypt into Canaan, which was guarded by Egyptian forts. Instead they went 'around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea,' verse 18. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew name is Yam Suph, often rendered 'Sea of Reeds.' The same name is used for the Gulf of Aqaba, 1 Kings 9:26, and many take the 'Red Sea' of Numbers 33:10 to be the Gulf of Suez, so the term seems to cover a range of waters east of Egypt. The exact place of the crossing is not known.

The place names in Exodus 14:2, Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon, have not been identified with certainty. Migdol means a tower or fortress, and several such places are known on Egypt's eastern frontier. Baal-zephon bears the name of a Canaanite god, Baal of Zaphon, associated with storms and the sea and honoured in Egypt as well. Israel was told to camp 'directly opposite' it, and the LORD would defeat Egypt's army at a place named for a god of the sea.

The chariot was the elite weapon of the age. Pharaoh took '600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt,' verse 7. To a people on foot, with women, children and flocks, such a force was overwhelming. The 'morning watch' of verse 24 was the last part of the night, before daybreak, a time used for surprise attacks, 1 Samuel 11:11.

The carrying of Joseph's bones, Exodus 13:19, fulfils the oath of Genesis 50:25. They would be buried at last at Shechem, Joshua 24:32. The pillar of cloud and fire of Exodus 13:21-22 would stay with Israel through the wilderness and later rest on the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34-38 and Numbers 9:15-23.
context.canonical:
The crossing of the sea became the defining memory of Israel's faith. The Song of Moses celebrates it at once, Exodus 15:1-21, and its opening line is sung again by Miriam, Exodus 15:21. When Israel crossed the Jordan, Joshua drew the parallel explicitly: 'the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you... just as He did to the Red Sea,' Joshua 4:23. Rahab tells the spies that Canaan had heard 'how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea,' Joshua 2:10.

The psalms return to it repeatedly. Psalm 66:6 says 'He turned the sea into dry land.' Psalm 77:16-20 pictures the waters seeing God and trembling, and says 'Your path led through the sea... but Your footprints were not to be found.' Psalm 78:13 and 106:7-12 retell it, the latter admitting that 'they rebelled by the sea' before God saved them 'for the sake of His name.' Psalm 114:3 has the sea look and flee. Psalm 136:13-15 gives each stage its own line of praise. Nehemiah 9:11 recalls it in Israel's great prayer of confession.

The prophets use the sea crossing to promise a new exodus. Isaiah 43:16-19 describes the LORD 'who makes a way in the sea' and then says, 'Behold, I am about to do something new.' Isaiah 51:9-11 links the dividing of the sea with the defeat of the chaos monster and with the return of 'the redeemed of the LORD.' Isaiah 63:11-13 asks, 'Where is He who brought them through the sea?'

In the New Testament Paul says Israel 'passed through the sea' and was 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. Hebrews 11:29 says 'By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land.' In the Gospels Jesus rebukes the sea, Mark 4:39, and walks on it, Mark 6:48-50, doing what the psalms attribute to the LORD alone. Revelation 15:2-3 shows the victors standing beside a sea of glass singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that its salvation was the LORD's work from beginning to end. God chose the route, verse 17. God placed Israel in what looked like a trap, verse 2. God hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he would pursue, verse 4. God moved the pillar to guard the camp, verse 19, drove back the sea, verse 21, jammed the chariot wheels, verse 25, and swept the Egyptians into the waters, verse 27. Israel's part was to be still, verse 14, and to go forward when told, verse 15.

He also wanted them to see the purpose. The LORD would 'gain honor' through Pharaoh, verses 4, 17 and 18, and both Egypt and Israel would come to know who He is. The crossing was not only a rescue but a revelation.

And he wanted a people who would respond with faith. Verse 31 records the goal: 'the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.' The same people who had accused Moses in verses 11 and 12 now trust him. Israel would face many more impossible situations in the wilderness and in the land, and the memory of the sea was meant to steady them. Whenever they were tempted to say 'it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians,' verse 12, they were to remember what the LORD had done at the sea.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The crossing is narrative, a unique act of God in Israel's history, and it does not promise that believers will always escape danger by miracle. Hebrews 11 places the sea crossing, verse 29, in the same chapter as those who 'were tortured' and 'put to death by the sword,' Hebrews 11:35-37. Faith sometimes sees the sea divided and sometimes does not.

Some of the words in the passage do carry instruction. 'Do not be afraid. Stand firm,' verse 13, and 'The LORD will fight for you,' verse 14, are echoed as words of encouragement to later generations, 2 Chronicles 20:17 and Deuteronomy 1:30. But verse 15 balances verse 14: 'Tell the Israelites to go forward.' Stillness does not mean passivity; it means refusing to trust one's own strength while obeying God's command.

The New Testament applies the passage chiefly to salvation in Christ and to baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, and it also uses Israel's failure after the crossing as a warning, 1 Corinthians 10:5-11. The lesson is not only that God saves the helpless, but that those who have been brought through the waters must go on trusting Him in the wilderness.

debates.question: How should the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in verses 4, 8 and 17 be understood alongside his earlier self-hardening?

views.label: A confirming judgment
views.case: By this stage Pharaoh had hardened his own heart repeatedly through the plagues, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32. God's hardening here confirms him in the rebellion he had already chosen. Paul's words that God 'gave them over' to their own desires, Romans 1:24, describe the same pattern of judgment.

views.label: A sovereign act for God's glory
views.case: The text states plainly that God hardens Pharaoh so that He will gain honor through Pharaoh's defeat, verse 4. Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh, 'I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you,' and concludes that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:17-18.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm real human responsibility and real divine sovereignty together. Pharaoh is never portrayed as an innocent puppet, since in verse 5 he and his officials freely decide to pursue, and God's purposes are never thwarted by human defiance.

debates.question: Where did the crossing happen, and how are the natural and miraculous elements related?

views.label: A miraculous parting at a major body of water
views.case: The text speaks of 'walls of water on their right and on their left,' verses 22 and 29, and of an entire army drowned, verse 28. Psalm 78:13 says 'He set the waters upright like a wall.' On this reading the crossing took place at a deep sea, such as an arm of the Gulf of Suez, and the event cannot be explained by natural means.

views.label: God using natural means at a reed marsh or lake
views.case: The Hebrew Yam Suph can mean 'Sea of Reeds,' as the BSB footnote notes, and some place the crossing at one of the shallow lakes east of the Nile delta. Verse 21 says the LORD used 'a strong east wind' all night. On this view God worked through wind and water, with the miracle lying in the timing and power of what He did.

debates.bearing: The text itself holds both together. It names the east wind and it describes walls of water and a drowned army. Whatever the location, the God who uses wind is still the one who divides the sea, and the timing, the protection of Israel, and the destruction of Egypt are all His work.

debates.question: Who is 'the angel of God' in verse 19?

views.label: The LORD Himself appearing
views.case: The angel moves with the pillar, verse 19, and verse 24 says the LORD looked down 'from the pillar of fire and cloud.' Elsewhere the angel of the LORD speaks as God, Exodus 3:2-6. Many in the church have seen here an appearance of the Son before His incarnation, especially since Paul says the rock that followed Israel 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4.

views.label: A created messenger sent by God
views.case: The word means messenger, and Exodus 23:20 and 32:34 speak of God sending His angel before Israel, distinguishing the angel from the LORD who sends him. On this reading the angel is a high servant who carries out God's protection.

debates.bearing: The BSB footnote notes the possibility of 'Angel.' Either way the point is the same: the presence that led Israel now stands between them and their enemy. God guards His people from behind as well as leading them from in front, Isaiah 52:12.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 18 says Israel left Egypt 'arrayed for battle,' chamushim. The word is uncertain. It is used of the eastern tribes crossing the Jordan 'armed for battle,' Joshua 1:14 and 4:12, and some connect it with the number five, suggesting ranks or divisions. The BSB footnote records that the Septuagint instead reads 'in the fifth generation.' Either way, Israel looked like an army, but it was an army that would not fight.

Joseph's oath in 13:19 quotes Genesis 50:25: 'God will surely attend to you,' paqod yifqod, the verb doubled for emphasis. The same doubled verb is God's message at the burning bush, 'I have surely attended to you,' Exodus 3:16. Moses carries the bones of the man who believed the promise, and he carries them because God had kept it.

The 'Red Sea' of 13:18 is Yam Suph. Suph is the word for the 'reeds' among which Moses' basket was placed on the Nile, Exodus 2:3 and 2:5, and for the 'seaweed' that wrapped Jonah's head, Jonah 2:5. The child who was saved among the suph now leads the nation through the Yam Suph.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart in verses 4, 8 and 17 uses chazaq, 'to strengthen' or 'stiffen,' as the footnote says. And the LORD says, 'I will gain honor,' ikkavedah, from kaved, 'to be heavy' or 'weighty.' The same root had described Pharaoh's heart as 'unyielding,' Exodus 7:14, and 'hardened,' Exodus 8:15. The play on words is deliberate. Pharaoh had made his heart heavy against God; now God makes Himself heavy, glorious, through Pharaoh.

In verse 8 Israel marches out 'defiantly,' literally 'with an upraised hand,' beyad ramah, as the footnote explains. Numbers 33:3 uses the same phrase of the exodus. But in Numbers 15:30 the same phrase describes the one who 'sins defiantly' against the LORD. The upraised hand can be the boldness of the redeemed or the arrogance of the rebel.

In verse 14, 'you need only to be still' is tacharishun, from charash, 'to be silent.' Israel had been crying out, verse 10, and accusing Moses, verses 11 and 12. The command is not only to stop moving but to stop speaking.

Verse 21 uses two words for the ground the sea became: charavah, 'dry land,' and yabbashah, 'dry ground,' the second repeated in verses 16, 22 and 29. Yabbashah is the word of Genesis 1:9, 'so that the dry land may appear.' The God who separated sea from dry land at creation does it again at the sea. The 'strong east wind' echoes the wind that brought the locusts, Exodus 10:13, and Genesis 8:1, where God 'sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside.'

In verse 24 the LORD 'threw their camp into confusion,' from hamam, a verb used in accounts of the LORD's battles, Joshua 10:10 and 1 Samuel 7:10. In verse 27 the LORD 'swept' the Egyptians into the sea, from na'ar, 'to shake off,' the verb Psalm 136:15 uses of the same event.

Finally, verse 30 says 'the LORD saved Israel,' vayyosha, from yasha, the root of yeshu'ah in verse 13. Earlier in the book Moses 'rose up to help' the daughters of Jethro, Exodus 2:17, with the same verb. And the 'great power' of verse 31 is literally 'the great hand,' hayyad haggedolah. Verse 30 had just spoken of 'the hand of the Egyptians.' Israel is saved from one hand by a greater one.

typology.fulfillment: Paul says Israel was 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:2. The crossing united Israel to the mediator God had given and separated them for good from the power of Egypt. Christian baptism is baptism 'into Christ Jesus' and 'into His death,' Romans 6:3, so that believers are buried with Him and raised to 'walk in newness of life,' Romans 6:4. The escalation is that Israel passed through water and was rescued from Pharaoh, while believers are united to Christ in death and resurrection and rescued from sin. The type falls short, as Paul warns, because many who crossed the sea still perished in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:5.

typology.type: The pillar of cloud and fire, Exodus 13:21-22 and 14:19-20
typology.fulfillment: The visible presence of God led Israel by day and night and then stood between Israel and Egypt, giving light to one camp and darkness to the other. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12, words spoken in the setting of the Feast of Tabernacles, John 7:2, which remembered the wilderness journey. John says the Word 'made His dwelling among us' and 'we have seen His glory,' John 1:14. The escalation is that God's presence no longer hovers above His people in a cloud but has taken flesh and, by the Spirit, dwells within them.

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea at God's command, and the people 'believed in Him and in His servant Moses.' Hebrews says 'Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's house,' but 'Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5-6. Moses was an instrument of salvation; Christ is its author, Hebrews 2:10. The escalation is that Moses stood above the water while God acted, whereas Jesus went down into death Himself and came up victorious. The type falls short because Moses himself later failed and did not enter the land, Numbers 20:12, while Christ leads His people all the way home.

typology.type: The enemy destroyed in the waters, Exodus 14:27-28
typology.fulfillment: The army that held Israel in bondage was destroyed completely, and 'not one of them survived.' Micah 7:19 uses the image for sin itself: 'You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' Paul says that at the cross Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and made 'a public spectacle of them,' Colossians 2:15, and that believers have been rescued 'from the dominion of darkness,' Colossians 1:13. The escalation is that the enemy defeated in Christ is not a human army but sin, death and the devil, Hebrews 2:14-15, whose defeat will be final, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: The song beside the sea, Exodus 14:31 and 15:1
typology.fulfillment: The crossing ends with a people who fear and believe, and in the next verse they sing. Revelation shows the victors standing beside 'a sea of glass mixed with fire,' singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:2-3. The redeemed of every age join the song first sung at the Red Sea, but its subject is now the Lamb's victory. The type reaches its end in the new creation, where 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1, and nothing threatening remains between God's people and His presence.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the Gospels' portraits of Jesus and the sea. In the Old Testament, commanding the sea is the LORD's prerogative. Job says God alone 'treads on the waves of the sea,' Job 9:8, and Psalm 106:9 says 'He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up.' In Mark 4:39 Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and the disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' In Mark 6:48-50 He comes to them 'walking on the sea' in the fourth watch of the night, the last watch before dawn, the same part of the night as the 'morning watch' in which the LORD looked down on Egypt's army, Exodus 14:24, and says, 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid,' the same reassurance Moses gave at the sea, Exodus 14:13. Mark does not spell out the link, but the pattern invites the question the disciples asked. Jesus does what only the God of the exodus does.

It leads to Christ through the language of salvation. Moses promised the people 'the LORD's salvation,' verse 13, and verse 30 says 'the LORD saved Israel.' Zechariah's song at the birth of John the Baptist speaks of God raising up 'a horn of salvation' in the house of David and of 'salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,' Luke 1:69-71, words close to Psalm 106:10. The angel tells Joseph to name the child Jesus, 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. The salvation of the sea becomes the salvation of the Saviour, and the enemy is no longer Egypt but sin.

It leads to Christ through the logic of a mediator. Israel could do nothing to open the sea; Moses could only stretch out his hand as God commanded. The New Testament describes Christ as the one mediator between God and humanity, 1 Timothy 2:5, and as the Son over God's house where Moses was a servant, Hebrews 3:5-6. At the sea Israel 'believed in Him and in His servant Moses,' verse 31. In the gospel, faith in God and faith in His Son are joined still more closely: 'You believe in God; believe in Me as well,' John 14:1.

It leads to Christ through death and new life. Paul's reading of the crossing as a baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, implies that Israel passed through the place of death and came out alive. Christians are baptized into Christ's death and raised with Him, Romans 6:3-4. Jesus Himself called His coming death a baptism, 'I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!' Luke 12:50. He did not stand above the waters like Moses; He went down into them, bearing the judgment, and rose on the other side.

A caution is in order. Not every detail of the passage, the chariot wheels, the camp at Pi-hahiroth, is a picture of Christ. The links above are the ones the New Testament itself draws or that grow from its own use of exodus language. What the passage gives is the shape of salvation: a helpless people, an enemy too strong for them, a God who fights, a mediator who obeys, and a way opened where there was no way. In Christ that shape is filled in completely.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is His wise guidance. He did not lead Israel by the shorter road, 'For God said, If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt,' Exodus 13:17. God knew the weakness of the people He had rescued and chose the longer way to protect them. His routes are not always the quickest, but they are always suited to those He leads.

It shows His presence. The pillar of cloud and fire 'went before them,' and it never 'left its place before the people,' Exodus 13:21-22. Then, when the danger came from behind, the angel of God and the pillar moved to stand between Israel and Egypt, Exodus 14:19-20. God is not only ahead of His people; He is also their rear guard, as Isaiah 52:12 later says. The same cloud that lit the night for Israel was darkness to Egypt, as in the ninth plague, Exodus 10:23. God's presence is light for His people and judgment for His enemies.

It shows His sovereignty. God tells Israel to turn back and camp in what seems a trap, verse 2. He predicts Pharaoh's thoughts, verse 3. He hardens Pharaoh's heart, verses 4, 8 and 17, and uses the pursuit to accomplish His purpose. Even Pharaoh's free choice, verse 5, serves God's plan. And His rule extends over nature: the wind blows at His command, the sea divides, the chariot wheels fail.

It shows Him as a warrior. 'The LORD will fight for you,' verse 14. The Egyptians confess it in verse 25, 'the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt,' and the song that follows declares, 'The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name,' Exodus 15:3. This is no tribal deity fighting for territory. He fights to deliver the oppressed and to judge the oppressor, and He fights alone.

It shows His concern for His glory. He will 'gain honor' through Pharaoh, verses 4, 17 and 18, and the Egyptians 'will know that I am the LORD.' This is not vanity. God's glory is the display of who He truly is, and for Egypt and Israel alike, knowing Him rightly is the greatest good. His glory and His people's rescue are achieved in the same act.

It shows His patience. Israel's accusation in verses 11 and 12 is bitter and faithless, yet God does not answer it with rebuke. He answers it with salvation. Psalm 106:7-8 notes that 'they rebelled by the sea,' and yet 'He saved them for the sake of His name.'

For worship, the passage calls for fear and faith, the response of verse 31. It also teaches a kind of stillness. Before a God who fights for His people, the right posture is to stop striving in our own strength, to stop accusing, and to move forward when He says go, trusting that He will make a way through what seems impassable.

crossReferences.note: Joseph, dying in Egypt, tells his brothers that God will surely attend to them and bring them to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and makes them swear to carry his bones. Exodus 13:19 records the oath kept. The man who trusted God's promise is carried out of Egypt when the promise comes true.

Moses and Israel sing about the event just narrated. 'The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea,' and 'the LORD is a warrior.' The song adds the image of the waters piling up at the blast of God's nostrils, verse 8, giving poetic voice to the walls of water of Exodus 14:22.

At the Jordan Joshua tells Israel to explain the memorial stones to their children: the LORD dried up the Jordan 'just as He did to the Red Sea.' The second crossing is modelled on the first, and its purpose is the same, that all peoples may know the hand of the LORD is mighty.

The psalmist, in distress, remembers the sea. The waters saw God and swirled, His path led through the mighty waters, but His footprints were not to be found, and He led His people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. The crossing becomes a comfort when God seems hidden.

The psalm confesses that Israel rebelled by the Red Sea, yet God saved them 'for the sake of His name,' rebuked the sea, and redeemed them from the enemy. Then 'they believed His promises and sang His praise.' It retells Exodus 14 as a story of grace to the undeserving.

The LORD describes Himself as the one 'who makes a way in the sea' and brings out chariots and horses to lie down, never to rise. Then He says, 'Behold, I am about to do something new.' Isaiah uses the Red Sea as a pattern for a greater act of salvation to come.

The prophet calls on the arm of the LORD to wake as in days past, when it dried up the sea and 'made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over.' The same God will bring the redeemed back to Zion with singing. The exodus becomes the promise of return from exile.

Paul says Israel's forefathers were all under the cloud and all passed through the sea, 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.' Yet God was not pleased with most of them, and they fell in the wilderness. The crossing is a picture of baptism, and Israel's later failure is a warning to the baptized.

'By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned.' Hebrews treats Israel's walking forward in Exodus 14:22 as an act of faith, and it draws the contrast between faith and presumption in the same sea.

Jesus comes to His disciples in the fourth watch of the night, walking on the sea, and says, 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.' He does what the Old Testament reserves for God, and He speaks the words of Exodus 14:13. The disciples' fear gives way, as Israel's did, to astonishment at who He is.

Facing a vast army, Jehoshaphat's people hear, 'You need not fight this battle. Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf.' The words of Exodus 14:13-14 are repeated for a later generation, showing that the sea taught Israel how to face every overwhelming enemy.

John sees those who conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb.' The victory song first sung on the shore of the Red Sea becomes the song of the redeemed at the end of history, now centred on the Lamb.

study.oneStory:
The sea has been a threat in Scripture from the opening verses. In Genesis 1:2 darkness lay 'over the surface of the deep,' and God brought order by separating the waters and letting 'the dry land' appear, Genesis 1:9. In the flood the waters returned to undo creation, until God 'sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside,' Genesis 8:1. At the Red Sea the same pattern returns. Wind drives back the waters, dry ground appears, and a people passes from death to life. The exodus is presented as a new act of creation.

The crossing also completes the break with Egypt. The Passover had spared Israel's firstborn and Pharaoh had let them go, but only at the sea is his power over them finally destroyed. The people who had been slaves see their oppressors 'dead on the shore,' verse 30. From here the story turns toward Sinai, where the redeemed people will receive the covenant, and toward the land where God will plant them. But the wilderness will show that a people brought through the waters can still lack faith, and the rest of the Pentateuch is the story of God's patience with them.

The memory of the sea shapes everything that follows. Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground, Joshua 3:17. The psalms sing of the sea again and again. When Israel is in exile, the prophets promise a new exodus: the LORD who made a way in the sea will make a way in the wilderness, Isaiah 43:16-19, and the redeemed will return to Zion with singing, Isaiah 51:11.

That new exodus comes in Christ. He rebukes the sea and walks on it. He calls His death a baptism, Luke 12:50, and He passes through death and rises. Those united to Him in baptism are brought through with Him, Romans 6:4, rescued from the dominion of darkness and brought into the kingdom of God's Son, Colossians 1:13.

The story ends with the sea itself removed. Revelation shows the redeemed standing beside a sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, Revelation 15:3. And in the new creation John writes, 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1. Every threat that the waters represented, chaos, death and the enemy, is gone. The people who once stood terrified on the shore will live forever in the presence of the God who fought for them, with nothing left between them and Him.

sermon.title: The Great Escape
sermon.why: Preached on Exodus 14:11-31, Keller draws out how the Red Sea crossing pictures salvation as bondage with layers, a crossing accomplished by grace, and a mediator through whom deliverance comes, reading the whole episode through a Christ-centered lens.

quiz.q: Why did God lead Israel by the longer wilderness road instead of the shorter route through Philistine territory?

options.text: So that facing war too soon would not make the people change their minds and return to Egypt.
options.note: Verse 17 gives this exact reason for God's chosen route.

options.text: Because the shorter road no longer existed.
options.note: The text gives a pastoral, protective reason, not a geographical impossibility.

options.text: Because Moses preferred the wilderness route personally.
options.note: The decision is explicitly God's, made for the people's own good, not Moses' personal preference.

options.text: There is no stated reason for the route chosen.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly explains God's reasoning.

quiz.q: What did Moses tell the terrified people to do as Pharaoh's army approached?

options.text: Stand firm, be still, and watch the LORD fight for them and save them.
options.note: Verses 13 to 14 give this exact instruction, faith expressed as stillness before God's action.

options.text: Arm themselves and prepare to fight the Egyptian army.
options.note: Moses tells them the opposite: the LORD will fight for them, they need only be still.

options.text: Scatter into the wilderness in different directions.
options.note: Moses calls for unified trust and stillness, not scattering in panic.

options.text: Surrender immediately to Pharaoh's forces.
options.note: Moses promises deliverance, not surrender.

quiz.q: How did the LORD divide the sea, according to verse 21?

options.text: By driving it back all that night with a strong east wind, so the waters were divided and the ground became dry.
options.note: The text specifies this means, a strong east wind, alongside Moses stretching out his hand.

options.text: By an earthquake that split the seabed instantly.
options.note: The text specifies a strong wind driving back the water overnight, not an earthquake.

options.text: The sea simply evaporated over several days.
options.note: The text describes a single overnight event, not a gradual evaporation.

options.text: The text does not describe how the sea was divided.
options.note: Verse 21 gives a specific description of the means, wind driving back the waters.

quiz.q: What happened to the pursuing Egyptian army?

options.text: The sea returned over them and not one of them survived.
options.note: Verse 28 states this outcome plainly.

options.text: They turned back safely before entering the seabed.
options.note: The Egyptians did follow into the sea, verse 23, and were destroyed when the waters returned.

options.text: They were captured and enslaved by Israel.
options.note: The text describes destruction by the returning sea, not capture.

options.text: Only Pharaoh himself drowned; the rest of the army survived.
options.note: The text says not one of the pursuing army survived.

quiz.q: What was the result in Israel after seeing this display of God's power?

options.text: They feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.
options.note: Verse 31 states this directly, fear and faith flowing from what they had witnessed.

options.text: They immediately began to worship the Egyptian gods out of terror.
options.note: The opposite occurs; they fear and believe in the LORD, not Egypt's gods.

options.text: They demanded to return to Egypt at once.
options.note: That grumbling recurs later in the wilderness, but this verse describes a moment of fear and faith, not a request to return.

options.text: No lasting response is recorded.
options.note: Verse 31 explicitly records their fear and belief.

questions: Israel panicked the moment the danger looked overwhelming, even after everything they had already seen God do. What overwhelming situation right now is tempting you to forget what God has already proven about Himself?
Moses told the people that all they had to do was stand still and watch the LORD fight for them. Where do you need to stop striving in your own strength and simply trust God to act on your behalf?

God deliberately chose the longer, harder road to protect Israel from a fight they were not ready for. Can you see a hard or slow path in your own life that might actually be God's protection rather than His neglect?

The Egyptians said, 'the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt,' even as they drowned. What does it mean for you that God's power to save His people is inseparable from His power to judge those who oppose them?

Fear and faith are named together as Israel's response at the shore, a right fear of God producing real trust. How might a deeper reverence for who God is actually strengthen, rather than weaken, your faith this week?

translationNotes.note: Arrayed for battle can also be rendered in orderly ranks or by fifties, describing an organized departure rather than a chaotic flight, though the Hebrew term's precise meaning is debated.
The place names Pi-hahiroth, Migdol, and Baal-zephon are precise enough that ancient readers could locate the crossing, though their exact modern identification remains uncertain.

A strong east wind is a genuine meteorological description, yet the text is clear the timing, intensity, and result were entirely under God's sovereign control, an act of both nature and miracle together.
